analysis.one_liner: Cuts the standard workweek to 32 hours, with overtime pay required beyond that.
analysis.headline: The bill to shorten the standard workweek to 32 hours was introduced in March 2024, referred to the Senate labor committee where a hearing was held, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the federal overtime law so that most hourly workers must be paid time-and-a-half for any hours beyond 32 in a week, phased in over four years (38, then 36, then 34, then 32 hours). It would also require overtime pay after 8 hours in a day and double pay after 12 hours, and it forbids employers from cutting a worker's pay rate or benefits when the new rules take effect. The bill was sent to the Senate committee that handles labor law, which held a hearing on it, but no committee vote and no floor vote ever happened before the two-year Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act who regularly work more than 32 hours a week: they would either get a shorter week at the same pay (because the bill bars benefit or rate cuts) or earn overtime premiums of 1.5x to 2x their regular rate for the extra hours [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers putting in long weeks

how_it_helps.text: Lowers the overtime threshold from 40 hours to 32 hours per week, phased in over four years at 38, 36, 34, and finally 32 hours, so hours beyond that must be paid at 1.5 times the regular rate [S2].
Adds daily overtime rules: time-and-a-half after 8 hours in a workday and double pay after 12 hours [S2].

Prohibits employers from reducing an employee's total compensation rate, regular rate, or any other benefit because the employee is newly covered by the lower threshold, protecting workers from a pay cut when the law changes [S2].
Extends the same 32-hour rule to the special overtime provisions in section 7(l) of the Fair Labor Standards Act (covering certain hospital and residential-care workers) [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, which would either absorb overtime premiums for hours past 32, hire additional workers to cover the same output, or restructure schedules; these costs could be passed on through prices or reduced flexibility [S2].

drawbacks.text: Businesses that rely on long hourly shifts would face sharply higher labor costs; a common objection is that some employers would respond by capping workers at 32 hours or shifting work to more, lower-paid part-time hires rather than paying overtime [S2].

The bill applies the same threshold to covered employees regardless of industry, so it does not tailor the transition for sectors like healthcare, manufacturing, or logistics where 40-plus-hour schedules are standard; costs would land within roughly 180 days for newly covered groups at the first 38-hour step [S2].

The anti-cutback provision protects pay rates and benefits but does not guarantee total weekly earnings for workers whose hours are cut below 32, so some workers could end up with fewer paid hours [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers who regularly work long weeks, the bill offers a genuine choice between a shorter week at protected pay and premium pay for extra hours — a substantial benefit. The main cost falls on employers, and the strongest honest objection is that some would avoid the premiums by limiting hours below 32, which the bill's pay-rate protection cannot fully prevent. It is a straightforward redistribution of scheduling power toward workers, but its design leaves room for evasion.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate's labor committee, which held a hearing on it, but the committee never voted on it and it never reached the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the Thirty-Two Hour Workweek Act in the Senate on March 14, 2024, joined by Sen. Laphonza Butler, with one Democratic cosponsor [S1][S2][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S1][S4].
The HELP Committee held a hearing at which the bill was discussed (printed as S.Hrg. 118-329), but the committee never marked up or voted on the bill [S4].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber, and it died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that would have faced new overtime costs beyond 32 hours a week are better off, since the bill died without a vote and no similar change became law in the 118th Congress.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator (VT), bill sponsor and Chairman of the Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, and as HELP chairman presided over a committee hearing at which it was discussed; did not schedule a committee vote on it.

for.name: Sen. Laphonza Butler
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders in introducing the bill.

for.name: Senate HELP Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill (S.Hrg. 118-329) but took no further action and never voted it out of committee.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a debate or vote during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored or supported the bill; with only two sponsors, there was never a realistic path to the 60 votes needed to advance most legislation past a filibuster in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had no Republican support: Sanders, an independent who caucuses with Democrats, and one Democratic cosponsor were its only backers, and no vote was ever held in either chamber.

industries.industry: Hourly-wage employers (retail, food service, warehousing, manufacturing, healthcare support)
industries.note: The bill would require overtime premiums for hours past 32 a week and past 8 a day, raising labor costs or forcing shorter schedules. Workers in those sectors stand to gain the same money or more free time, so the industry's interest runs against theirs.

Higher overtime costs at client firms could push employers toward more hires, potentially increasing demand for staffing services, but the anti-cutback rule and premium pay would also raise costs for the agencies' own hourly workers.

The bill specifically extends the 32-hour overtime threshold to the section 7(l) provisions covering hospital and residential-care employees, a sector that commonly uses long shifts; overtime premiums beyond 32 hours would raise operating costs.
